# winwright

> A Windows UI test framework for .NET 10 (`net10.0-windows`). It drives a desktop
> application through UI Automation and Win32, derives its expectations from the
> application's own declarations, and answers in four verdicts rather than two — so a check
> that could not be evaluated is named in the summary rather than left out of the count.
> The engine has no external dependency, and the application under test references at most
> one optional package.

It exists because of one measurement. A suite reported a pass with no failures and a total
of 352 where the run before it had 374 — twenty-two checks gone, the host had died partway
through, and the only sign was a number nobody had a reason to read.

## For agents

This site answers a coding agent in files it can grep, not only in hydrated markup. Every
route has a Markdown twin beside it — the same page, converted from the same render, with
the navigation, the footer and the call to action dropped. Read `<route>/index.md` instead
of the HTML: the landing page is
[`/index.md`](https://alegauss.github.io/winwright/index.md). The full list of routes,
their twins and their byte sizes is in
[`manifest.json`](https://alegauss.github.io/winwright/manifest.json).

## The verdict, and the exit code

The enum member values **are** the process exit codes — a mapping written twice is a mapping
that drifts, and CI reads the number rather than the word.

| Code | Outcome | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | `Passed` | Every assertion ran, and every one of them held. |
| `1` | `Failed` | At least one assertion ran and did not hold. |
| `2` | `Degraded` | Everything that ran passed, and something could not be evaluated at all. |
| `3` | `Broken` | The harness threw. What it says is about this tool, not about your application. |

`2` is the reason this project exists. An assertion whose precondition was absent did not
pass and did not fail — it never ran, it is named in the summary by name, and collapsing it
into either of the other two is the thing winwright will not do. `3` outranks the rest,
because a reader told the build failed opens the wrong repository.

Three things a scenario meets often are holes rather than failures, and all of them are
about the desk rather than about your application: a foreground Windows would not grant, a
focus that left the application while a menu walk or a traversal was polling, and a
notification-area flyout the shell would not open.

Before the assertions, a run takes one reading of the machine: the desk it is on, which
binary it is driving, whether that binary is stale, the resolved language, the foreground,
the launch arguments, whether anything else is showing the application, and whether the desk
is this run's alone. Each is reported as measured, absent, or **not read**.

## The locator grammar

One grammar, written once, read the same way by every verb.

```
#saveButton                              the automation id
Button                                   the control type
Button#saveButton                        both
Button[name="Save as..."]                the name
Pane[class=Chrome_WidgetWin_1]           the window class
Button[pattern=Invoke]                   it must carry that pattern
Text[name="Statistics"][order=left]      the leftmost of the ones that match
MenuItem[order=top][index=2]             the second from the top
Window#main > Pane > Button#save         a descendant of, at any depth
```

`>` means **a descendant of**, not a direct child. That is a decision, not a shorthand: UI
Automation wraps controls in panes that differ between frameworks, between versions of one
framework, and between a maximised window and a restored one — so a direct-child locator is
the one that breaks on somebody else's machine. `Locator.Parse` refuses a locator that does
not parse, naming the position and the reason; `Locator.TryParse` answers without throwing.
Two elements matching one step is a refusal, not a first match, and a misspelt control type
is answered with the nearest name UI Automation actually has.

## Features

- **Locate** — resolve one look at a locator, the same polled to a deadline, or every
  element a step matches; inspect the control view under a window or an element as a tree or
  as lines a person reads; read what UI Automation says about one element and what each of
  its patterns holds.
- **Act** — invoke, toggle, set a value or a range, select, expand, collapse, through the
  control's own patterns. **A pattern act is the default and needs no foreground.** The verbs
  that synthesise input (pointer, keyboard, traversal) are marked as needing the foreground
  in a catalogue checked against the engine in both directions: a verb added without an entry
  is a red. Actionability answers whether an element can take an act at all and why not where
  it cannot; a preflight checks what every declared act needs against the tree before
  anything is pressed.
- **Menus and the notification area** — enter a menu bar the way a keyboard user does, walk
  to an entry, open a submenu, dismiss; the tray, the overflow flyout, the icons on either,
  and an icon's context menu. Finding an icon says which of the two happened — the icon is
  absent, or the flyout would not open.
- **Assert** — the expectation is derived, never typed. Labels come from the project's own
  language files, so switching the resolved language switches the expected set with it and a
  key none of the files carries refuses the run rather than matching nothing. Every
  expectation is falsifiable; a timed-out read is recorded as a reading that did not arrive
  rather than as a default that looks like data; a failing step carries the tree, the
  element's facts and what its patterns read.
- **Capture** — a picture that proves what it photographed. The z order above the window is
  enumerated and intersected with the copy rectangle in one pass; an overlap fails rather
  than crops and the refusal names the intruder, its process and the rectangle; a window with
  a system backdrop is refused because glass transmits what is behind it; a copy of exactly
  one colour is not a picture; a page still computing is not a report. Two renders of
  unchanged code are byte-identical, so no tolerance has to be chosen for a comparison to
  mean anything.
- **Scenarios** — a case is a data file: steps, locators, acts and expectations as fields,
  with the loop, the waits and the verdicts owned by the engine. Every field is validated at
  insertion, so a refusal costs a retry and never a deletion. Run a file, a case or a tag,
  and be told what was not run. Preconditions, fixtures and sampled environments are declared
  per case and passed to every launch the case makes. A window can be declared shareable.
  Each case carries the defect it exists to catch.
- **The project declaration** — `winwright.json`, found by walking up from where a run
  starts. Every key is optional; a reading that needs one this file does not declare is
  recorded as not taken, never quietly skipped. `destructive` names the entries that end the
  run, and a bare name is refused where the project ships more than one language, because a
  name is the field a translation rewrites.
- **The Claude Code plugin** — two commands in the repository wire every clone. The MCP
  tools carry this project's scenario schema as their input schema, so a case an agent
  writes is refused at insertion rather than at run time; the skill loads when a window is in
  play rather than on every turn; a hook denies a hand-written harness script and names the
  verb that replaces it.
- **The in-app half (optional)** — `Winwright.InApp`, taken by the application under test
  only if you want the readings a harness cannot take from outside the process: whether this
  process's idea of the display is trustworthy, an element rendered to a PNG (measured,
  arranged and updated in that order), the background a capture is drawn on from a brush the
  application declares, the laid-out tree and what was drawn, and every popup held open for
  as long as a run lasts. It references the engine not at all, and an application shipped to
  its users reports nothing and writes no file.

## Non-goals (stated, not accidental)

- Cross-platform — the whole engine is UI Automation and Win32.
- An external dependency in the engine.
- An assertion about individual pixels.
- A recorder that turns clicks into a scenario. The tool never writes the test.
- A service, a daemon or a database.
- A green that covers an assertion that did not run.

## Installation

The harness half goes in the project that drives the application:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Winwright" Version="0.1.0" />
```

The in-app half goes in the application under test, and only if you want the readings it can
only take from inside:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Winwright.InApp" Version="0.1.0" />
```

Windows, .NET 10, `net10.0-windows`. The in-app half needs `<UseWPF>true</UseWPF>`.

## Layout

- `src/Winwright` — the engine: locating, acting, asserting, capturing, tracing, verdicts,
  windowing, projects and scenarios. No package reference, deliberately.
- `src/Winwright.InApp` — the in-app half. No reference to the engine, deliberately.
- `src/Winwright.Fixture` — an application built to be hard to test, which is what every
  refusal in the engine is paired against.
- `tools/Winwright.RollCall` — the roll call, so a run short of what discovery found is not
  reported as a pass.
- `site/` — this site (Vite + React + Tailwind); its build emits this file, a Markdown twin
  per route and `manifest.json`.
- `docs/ROADMAP.md`, `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` — governed by
  [roadkeep](https://github.com/alegauss/roadkeep) and written by that tool, not by hand.

## Data and network

Nothing is uploaded, nothing is measured, and there is no account. A run is a process that
starts, observes, reports and stops; the store a case writes through is fingerprinted before
and compared after, so a run that changed the machine of whoever ran it is a refusal rather
than a surprise.
